2027-05-10.title: Seventh Monday of Resurrection
2027-05-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: God chose you as the first fruits for salvation
2027-05-10.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta), in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. The fourth day of the novena to the Holy Spirit. In the Latin calendar, St John of Avila, priest and doctor of the Church (optional memorial).
2027-05-10.verse: The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.
theo: It is noon in Samaria. “Jesus, tired out by his journey, was sitting by the well.” The Lord who has now ascended to the Father once sat tired on the edge of Jacob's well, in the heat of the day, and asked a woman for water: “Give me a drink.” She is astonished, for “Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans”, and a Jewish teacher did not usually speak alone with a woman of Samaria. Jesus crosses both walls at once. He is not ashamed to need something from her. That is how God often begins with us: not with a command but with a request. He asks for a little of our time, a little of our attention, a cup of water, so that he can give far more. “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman thinks of running water from a spring rather than the still water of the cistern. Jesus means something deeper: the gift of God himself.

She objects with the practical sense of a woman who has carried water every day of her life: “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep.” And she asks the great question: “Are you greater than our ancestor Jacob?” Jesus answers by comparing two kinds of water. “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but those who drink of the water that I will give them will never be thirsty. The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.” John explains later what this water is: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which believers in him were to receive; for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7:39). Now Jesus has been glorified. He has gone up to the Father, and the Spirit is about to be poured out. That is why we read this Gospel in the days of the novena. Every thirst we carry, for love, for meaning, for forgiveness, for peace, is in the end a thirst for God, and the Holy Spirit is the spring that God places inside us. The woman's first answer is still on the surface: “Sir, give me this water, so that I may never be thirsty or have to keep coming here to draw water.” But she has begun to ask, and the conversation that follows will make her the first missionary of her town.

Paul writes to the Thessalonians with gratitude, because the same Spirit has already been at work in them. “God chose you as the first fruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and through belief in the truth.” The first fruits were the first part of the harvest, offered to God as a promise of the rest. The young Church of Thessalonica was the first harvest in its city; the Syro-Malabar Church, born from the preaching of Thomas, was among the first fruits of the Gospel in India. Paul's advice to such a Church is simple: “So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by our letter.” The faith comes to us by the living voice of the Church and by the Scriptures together. Our Mar Thoma tradition, the prayers our grandparents taught us, the way our Church celebrates the Qurbana, are not dead customs; they are channels through which the living water has reached us. Paul ends with a blessing for these days of waiting: “may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and through grace gave us eternal comfort and good hope, comfort your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word.”
conn: Jacob bought a plot of land at Shechem, and it became the inheritance of Joseph's descendants (Genesis 33:18–20; Joshua 24:32); Jesus meets the woman at the well of the patriarchs.
“With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3).
“They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug out cisterns for themselves, cracked cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).
On the Cross the One who offered living water says, “I am thirsty” (John 19:28).
“Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.” John explains: “Now he said this about the Spirit” (John 7:38–39).
Let everyone who is thirsty come.
“And let everyone who is thirsty come. Let anyone who wishes take the water of life as a gift” (Revelation 22:17).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord who asked for a drink at the well gives us himself to drink: his Blood is the living water that becomes in us a spring gushing up to eternal life.
We bring to the altar our tiredness and our thirst, as the woman brought her empty jar, and we take home the Spirit who comforts and strengthens our hearts.
outline: Noon at Jacob's well: the tired Lord asks a woman for water.
God begins with a request, and crosses every wall.
The Spirit, the spring inside us, poured out after the Ascension.
Point 3 · Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions
First fruits, Mar Thoma heritage, and the eternal comfort of God.
An old family well in a Kerala courtyard that never dried, even in a hard summer.
“The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.”
live: In the novena today, tell the Lord honestly what you are thirsty for, and ask him for the living water of the Spirit.
Speak kindly this week with someone your family or community usually keeps at a distance.
Hold fast to the traditions (2 Thessalonians 2:15)
Teach a child one prayer of our Church this week, or explain one part of the Qurbana.
Offer water or a cool drink to a delivery worker, a labourer or a guest today, in the name of Christ.
fathers: He who asked for a drink was thirsting for her faith. He asked for water and promised water; he asked as one in need, and he promised as one who could fill her. He came tired to the well, he who is the strength of the weak, so that he might find the one who was lost.

The tradition of the apostles, made known throughout the whole world, can be found in every Church by those who wish to see the truth. The Church, like a rich storehouse, has received from the apostles all that belongs to the truth, so that whoever will may draw from her the water of life.
magis: Jesus thirsts; his asking arises from the depths of God's desire for us. Whether we realize it or not, prayer is the encounter of God's thirst with ours. God thirsts that we may thirst for him.
Water signifies the Holy Spirit's action in Baptism. The Spirit is also personally the living water welling up from Christ crucified as its source and welling up in us to eternal life.

The living transmission accomplished in the Holy Spirit is called Tradition. Tradition and Scripture are bound closely together: flowing from the same divine wellspring, they make up a single sacred deposit of the faith.
saints: 7–13 May: the days after the Ascension of our Lord (Thursday 6 May), when the apostles waited in prayer for the Holy Spirit “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit from Friday 7 to Saturday 15 May, the eve of Pentecost. Fri 7: First Friday. Sun 9: Seventh Sunday of Resurrection, the Sunday after the Ascension; the Latin Church in India celebrates the Ascension on this Sunday. Mon 10: in the Latin calendar, St John of Avila. Wed 12: in the Latin calendar, Sts Nereus and Achilleus and St Pancras. Thu 13: in the Latin calendar, Our Lady of Fatima. The Marian month of May continues (verify locally).
2027-05-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, tired from your journey you sat by the well and asked for a drink, so that you might give us the living water. Now you are glorified at the Father's right hand: pour out on us the Spirit you promised, and let him become in us a spring gushing up to eternal life. Satisfy our deepest thirst, help us to cross the walls that divide people, and keep us faithful to the traditions handed down to us from the apostles. Comfort our hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word. Amen. Alleluia!

quick: At Jacob's well the tired Lord asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, crossing every wall.
He promises living water: the Spirit, a spring gushing up to eternal life.
Paul: God chose you as first fruits; stand firm and hold fast to the traditions.
2027-05-10.action: Tell the Lord honestly what you are thirsty for, and offer a drink to someone in his name.
2027-05-10.question: From which wells am I trying to quench a thirst that only God can satisfy?
kidsaint: The Gospel does not tell us her name; an old Eastern tradition calls her Photini, which means ‘the shining one’. She came to the well at noon to draw water, and she met Jesus, who asked her for a drink. When she understood who he was, she left her water jar and ran to tell the whole town, ‘Come and see!’ Many people believed because of her. Lesson: when you meet Jesus, you can say to your friends, ‘Come and see!’
2027-05-10.special: Seventh Monday of Resurrection. Fourth day of the novena to the Holy Spirit. In the Latin calendar, St John of Avila.
term: From the Latin traditio, ‘handing on’ (in Greek paradosis). The Church's living transmission of the Gospel received from the apostles, in her teaching, life and worship, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. With Sacred Scripture it forms one deposit of the faith. Paul asks the Thessalonians to hold fast to what they were taught “either by word of mouth or by our letter”.

family.explain: Jesus was tired and thirsty, and he sat beside a well. A woman came to draw water, and Jesus asked her, ‘Please give me a drink.’ Then he told her about a special water that he gives: whoever drinks it will never be thirsty again! This water is the Holy Spirit, who fills our hearts with God's love. In a few days, at Pentecost, we will celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit.
family.intention: We pray for people who have no clean water to drink, and for all who are thirsty for God's love.
family.ask: Ask: “Who can we give a glass of water or a kind word to this week?”

illus: In an old house near Pala there is a well that the family says has never dried, not even in the drought summers when the river shrank to a stream. Neighbours came with pots, and the grandmother never sent anyone away. Once a city cousin asked why the well stayed full. The old woman said, ‘The water does not come from the top. It comes from a spring underneath that we cannot see.’ Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would be like that in us: not a bucket of water that runs out, but a hidden spring, ‘gushing up to eternal life’, from which others too can drink.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you sat tired by the well and asked for a drink. We come to you thirsty; give us the living water of your Spirit. Amen. Alleluia!
share: Jesus, tired out by his journey, was sitting by the well (John 4:6). How does it move me that the Lord knows tiredness?
If you knew the gift of God (John 4:10). What gift of God have I not yet understood or received?
Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again (John 4:13). What wells do I keep going back to that leave me thirsty?
Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Which tradition of our Church helps me most to stay close to God?
interc: For the Church, that she may offer the living water of Christ to all who thirst.
For those who are tired of life and have lost hope, that the Spirit may become a spring of new life in them.
For people divided by religion, caste or community, that the example of Jesus at the well may teach us to cross walls with respect.
For those who lack clean water, and for all who work to provide it.
For our families, that we may hand on the faith of our fathers with joy.
pm.close: Father, your Son gives the living water that quenches every thirst. Pour out your Spirit on us, keep us faithful to the faith handed down from the apostles, and comfort our hearts with good hope, through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, today the Gospel takes us to a well in Samaria at noon. Jesus is tired, and he sits down. A woman comes to draw water, and Jesus asks her: “Give me a drink.”

She is surprised. Jews and Samaritans did not mix, and a Jewish teacher did not talk alone with a Samaritan woman. But Jesus crosses those walls. He is not ashamed to ask. God often begins with us like this: not with an order, but with a request. He asks for a little of our time, so that he can give us much more.

Jesus says: “If you knew the gift of God,” you would have asked me, and I would have given you living water. Whoever drinks ordinary water will be thirsty again. But “the water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.” This living water is the Holy Spirit. Jesus has now gone up to the Father, and the Spirit is about to be poured out. In this novena, let us bring him our thirst.

Paul tells the Thessalonians: God chose you as first fruits. Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions you were taught. Our Church received the faith from St Thomas, and our grandparents handed it to us. These traditions are channels through which the living water has reached us. Let us keep them and hand them on.
The woman said, “Sir, give me this water.” Let that be our prayer today: Lord, give us this water. Fill us with your Spirit at Pentecost. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus was thirsty, and he asked a woman for water. Then he told her about a special water that he gives, the Holy Spirit.
When we pray, the Holy Spirit fills our heart like a little spring of water that never dries. Say today: ‘Jesus, give me your living water!’

The fourth day of the novena: the Lord who asks for a drink, the living water of the Spirit, and the traditions through which that water has reached us.

q: O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water.
A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”

sub: Every thirst is a thirst for God.

Let us bring him our thirst and keep the faith handed down to us.
